explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. Verse 3 says, "I have commanded My sanctified ones; I have even summoned My warriors…" Notice the word "even," like the list just got bigger. These are not folks who show up with oven mitts, and believe me, I have lost arguments to oven mitts.

Good guess, since this whole thing is a prophet's burden. But the verse names a different group. It says, "I have commanded My sanctified ones; I have even summoned My warriors…" Warriors are the ones summoned here.

I can see why a judge would feel right at home in this scene. But no judges show up in verse 3. The text says, "I have commanded My sanctified ones; I have even summoned My warriors…" So the second group is the warriors.

Yes, wrath. The warriors are summoned "to execute My wrath and exult in My triumph." That's a heavy word, so I'll just say it plainly: this burden is serious. Keep that word in your pocket, because it keeps coming back in this passage.

Mercy is a lovely word, friend, but it's not the one in this verse. The warriors are summoned "to execute My wrath and exult in My triumph." The word right there in verse 3 is wrath. I'd love to hand you the softer answer, but I only bake what the text says.

Law sounds official enough to fit, I'll give you that. But verse 3 says the warriors are summoned "to execute My wrath and exult in My triumph." The word is wrath. Nothing about law shows up in that line.

explanations.answer: The LORD of Hosts raising an army
explanations.explanation: That's it. Verse 4 says, "The LORD of Hosts is mobilizing an army for war." So all that noise on the mountains has one source. Quite a crowd, friend. My bakery has never once been that loud, and I include the day the timer went off right behind me.

explanations.answer: The kings of Egypt making a treaty
explanations.explanation: A treaty would be a calmer kind of uproar, wouldn't it? But Egypt isn't mentioned in this passage, and nobody is signing anything here. Verse 4 says, "The LORD of Hosts is mobilizing an army for war." That's what the uproar is.

explanations.answer: The tribes of Israel coming home
explanations.explanation: A homecoming would be a happy noise, friend. Not this one, though. The passage never mentions the tribes of Israel coming home. Verse 4 says, "The LORD of Hosts is mobilizing an army for war."
Country is right. Verse 5 says they are coming "to destroy the whole country." Look at that word "whole." It means the whole land, not a corner of it.
A temple is a big target, I know. But no temple is mentioned in verse 5. It says they are coming "to destroy the whole country." The word is country, friend.

Close, because an army is all over this verse. But the army is the one doing the coming. The LORD and the weapons of His wrath are coming "to destroy the whole country." That's the word that fits the blank.

explanations.answer: The Day of the LORD is near
explanations.explanation: You've got it. Verse 6 says, "Wail, for the Day of the LORD is near; it will come as destruction from the Almighty." The cry to wail comes with its reason attached. It's one of the big phrases of this passage, so you'll hear it again.

explanations.answer: The king of Babylon has died
explanations.explanation: That would give people a reason to wail, I'll admit. But this passage never says the king of Babylon has died. Verse 6 says, "Wail, for the Day of the LORD is near…" The Day of the LORD is the reason.

A lost harvest would make anybody wail. I once lost a whole batch to a distracted afternoon, so I understand. But nothing here says the harvest is lost. Verse 6 says, "Wail, for the Day of the LORD is near…"

Melt is right. Verse 7 says, "all hands will fall limp, and every man's heart will melt." It's a picture of fear taking the strength right out of people. My chocolate chips know a little about melting, but they've never melted from fear.
I wish it were that cheerful, friend. But verse 7 says, "all hands will fall limp, and every man's heart will melt." Rejoicing doesn't show up anywhere in that picture. The word is melt.

Hardening feels like a natural opposite, but the verse goes the other way. It says, "all hands will fall limp, and every man's heart will melt." Limp hands and melting hearts, friend. Nothing in this picture is hard.

Right. Verse 8 says, "Terror, pain, and anguish will seize them; they will writhe like a woman in labor." The picture is pain and fear that grab a person hard. Then the same verse says they will look at one another with faces flushed with fear.
A wounded soldier fits the battle scene, I know. But Isaiah picks a different picture. Verse 8 says, "they will writhe like a woman in labor." That's the comparison in the text.

A storm at sea is a scary picture, friend, but it's not the one Isaiah uses. The text says, "Terror, pain, and anguish will seize them; they will writhe like a woman in labor." The comparison is a woman in labor.

True. Verse 9 says the Day of the LORD is coming "to make the earth a desolation and to destroy the sinners within it." That's a hard line, so I won't dress it up. Isaiah says it plainly, and so do I.

This one is true, friend, so False isn't the answer. Verse 9 says the Day of the LORD is coming "to make the earth a desolation and to destroy the sinners within it." The sinners are named right there in the text.

The moon doesn't get to keep its glow here. Verse 10 says, "The rising sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light." So the statement is false. Not even the moon is shining on that day.

False is right, friend. Verse 10 says, "The rising sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light." Try finding a light switch in a sky like that. Sun, moon and stars are all dark in this picture.

That's the pair. Verse 11 says, "I will end the haughtiness of the arrogant and lay low the pride of the ruthless." Pride gets named twice in one verse, friend. The ones laid low are the proud, the arrogant and the ruthless.

No, the poor and the lowly aren't named here. Verse 11 says, "I will end the haughtiness of the arrogant and lay low the pride of the ruthless." The ones brought low are the arrogant and the ruthless, friend.

The weak and the weary don't appear in verse 11. The text says, "I will end the haughtiness of the arrogant and lay low the pride of the ruthless." So the other group is the arrogant and the ruthless.

explanations.answer: Very few people will be left
explanations.explanation: Yes. Verse 12 says, "I will make man scarcer than pure gold, and mankind rarer than the gold of Ophir." Gold is hard to find, so the picture is that people will be hard to find. Not many left, friend.
I see the gold and I see why your mind went there. But the gold is the measuring stick, not a prize. Verse 12 says, "I will make man scarcer than pure gold…" The picture is about people being scarce.

explanations.answer: Gold will run out in the land
explanations.explanation: Gold is in the verse, but it's not the thing running short. The text says, "I will make man scarcer than pure gold, and mankind rarer than the gold of Ophir." Man is the thing that gets scarce, friend. Gold is just the comparison.

People is right. Verse 14 says, "each will return to his own people, each will flee to his native land." Everyone heads back toward home. The verse also says they're like a hunted gazelle and a sheep without a shepherd.
A king gives people somewhere to run, I know. But verse 14 doesn't mention a king there. It says, "each will return to his own people, each will flee to his native land." The blank is people, friend.
Gods would be a surprising place to run, friend. But verse 14 never says that. It says, "each will return to his own people, each will flee to his native land." The word is people.
Silver and gold are the opposite of what moves these people. Verse 17 says the Medes "have no regard for silver and no desire for gold." So the statement is false. Treasure is not what draws them.

False is right. Verse 17 says, "Behold, I will stir up against them the Medes, who have no regard for silver and no desire for gold." Imagine a crowd that doesn't care about treasure, friend. That's what the text says about the Medes.

Sodom and Gomorrah, yes. Verse 19 says Babylon "will be overthrown by God like Sodom and Gomorrah." Babylon was called the jewel of the kingdoms, and that's the comparison Isaiah reaches for. A big fall for a big name, friend.
Good pair of city names, friend, but they're not in this verse. Verse 19 says Babylon "will be overthrown by God like Sodom and Gomorrah." Those are the two cities Isaiah names.
Those two are not in this passage. Verse 19 says Babylon "will be overthrown by God like Sodom and Gomorrah." Those are the two cities in the text, friend.

True. Verse 20 says, "She will never be inhabited or settled from generation to generation…" That word "never" is doing heavy lifting. And the next part says no nomad will pitch a tent there and no shepherd will rest a flock there.

This one is true, friend, so False isn't the answer. Verse 20 says, "She will never be inhabited or settled from generation to generation…" Not for a generation, and not for the ones after it either. Isaiah doesn't leave a door open.

Yes. Verse 21 says, "But desert creatures will lie down there, and howling creatures will fill her houses. Ostriches will dwell there, and wild goats will leap about." The old houses get a whole different crowd of residents. Nobody in that neighborhood is bringing a casserole, friend.

Lions and wolves would make a fierce guest list, but they aren't on this one. Verse 21 says, "But desert creatures will lie down there, and howling creatures will fill her houses. Ostriches will dwell there, and wild goats will leap about." So the answer is desert creatures and ostriches.

Eagles and ravens aren't named here, friend. Verse 21 says, "But desert creatures will lie down there, and howling creatures will fill her houses. Ostriches will dwell there, and wild goats will leap about." Desert creatures and ostriches are the ones who move in.
Isaiah says the opposite, friend. Verse 22 ends with, "Babylon's time is at hand, and her days will not be prolonged." Her days are not stretched out at all. So the statement is false.
False is right. Verse 22 closes with, "Babylon's time is at hand, and her days will not be prolonged." It's a short, firm last line. No extra years are promised there.
